claim: EXOC1 is a member of the Exocyst complex.
source: Here, we found that EXOC1, a member of the Exocyst complex, is important for the pseudopod formation of spermatogonia and spermatocyte syncytia in mice.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of EXOC1.

claim: EXOC1 is important for the pseudopod formation of spermatogonia in mice.
source: Here, we found that EXOC1, a member of the Exocyst complex, is important for the pseudopod formation of spermatogonia and spermatocyte syncytia in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: EXOC1 is important for spermatocyte syncytia in mice.
source: Here, we found that EXOC1, a member of the Exocyst complex, is important for the pseudopod formation of spermatogonia and spermatocyte syncytia in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: EXOC1 contributes to the pseudopod formation of spermatogonia by inactivating the Rho family small GTPase Rac1.
source: EXOC1 contributes to the pseudopod formation of spermatogonia by inactivating the Rho family small GTPase Rac1 and also functions in the spermatocyte syncytia with the SNARE proteins STX2 and SNAP23.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing increased active-Rac1 in Exoc1 cKO mice.

claim: EXOC1 functions in the spermatocyte syncytia with the SNARE proteins STX2 and SNAP23.
source: EXOC1 contributes to the pseudopod formation of spermatogonia by inactivating the Rho family small GTPase Rac1 and also functions in the spermatocyte syncytia with the SNARE proteins STX2 and SNAP23.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and phenotypic analysis.

claim: EXOC1 is known to bind to several cell morphogenesis factors.
source: Since EXOC1 is known to bind to several cell morphogenesis factors, this study is expected to be the starting point for the discovery of many morphological regulators of male germ cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Sperms are continuously produced in the seminiferous tubules throughout a male's life in mammalian testis.
source: In mammalian testis, sperms are continuously produced in the seminiferous tubules throughout a male's life.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: There are two types of cells in the seminiferous tubule: somatic cells (Sertoli cells) and male germ cells.
source: There are two types of cells in the seminiferous tubule, somatic cells (Sertoli cells) which support spermatogenesis and male germ cells which undergo various processes to become spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, and eventually spermatozoa.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The Sertoli cell tight junction (SCTJ) divides the seminiferous tubule into two compartments: the basal compartment and the luminal compartment.
source: Structurally, the Sertoli cell tight junction (SCTJ) divides the seminiferous tubule into two compartments, the basal compartment and the luminal compartment (Tsukita et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Spermatogonia cells are located in the basal compartment.
source: Spermatogonia cells are located in the basal compartment and undergo proliferation and differentiation by mitosis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Spermatogonia undergo proliferation and differentiation by mitosis.
source: Spermatogonia cells are located in the basal compartment and undergo proliferation and differentiation by mitosis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Cells that have differentiated into spermatocytes migrate to the luminal compartment.
source: The cells that have differentiated into spermatocytes migrate to the luminal compartment and differentiate into haploid spermatocytes by meiosis (Smith and Braun, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Spermatocytes differentiate into haploid spermatocytes by meiosis.
source: The cells that have differentiated into spermatocytes migrate to the luminal compartment and differentiate into haploid spermatocytes by meiosis (Smith and Braun, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Long-term stable spermatogenesis is supported by spermatogonial stem cells.
source: As this entire differentiation process is cyclical and continuous, long-term stable spermatogenesis is supported by spermatogonial stem cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Murine spermatogonia can be classified as undifferentiated and differentiating.
source: Murine spermatogonia are heterogeneous in their differential state and can be classified as undifferentiated and differentiating (Fayomi and Orwig, 2018; Suzuki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: During spermatogenesis, germ cells undergo an incomplete cytoplasmic division.
source: During spermatogenesis, germ cells undergo an incomplete cytoplasmic division.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In germ cells, the final separation is inhibited and they differentiate while maintaining intercellular bridges (ICBs).
source: In most somatic cell types, daughter cells completely separate from each other, but in germ cells, the final separation is inhibited and they differentiate while maintaining intercellular bridges (ICBs) (Iwamori et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Syncytia are thought to contribute to syncytial differentiation and maturation by the sharing of mRNAs and proteins that are halved during meiosis via ICB.
source: Such structures, called syncytia, are thought to contribute to syncytial differentiation and maturation by the sharing of mRNAs and proteins that are halved during meiosis via ICB (Morales et al., 2002; Fawcett et al., 1959).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Undifferentiated spermatogonia include Asingle as isolated cells, Apair as two connected syncytia, and Aaligned as three or more connected cells.
source: Undifferentiated spermatogonia are a morphologically heterogeneous population that includes Asingle as isolated cells, Apair as two connected syncytia, and Aaligned as three or more connected cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: A large number of stem cells that contribute to long-term spermatogenesis are included within the GFRα1+ undifferentiated spermatogonia.
source: Furthermore, a large number of stem cells that contribute to long-term spermatogenesis are included within the GFRα1+ undifferentiated spermatogonia (mainly Asingle and Apair, and fewer Aaligned), although whether the stem cell compartment comprises of all or only a subset of GFRα1+ population remains under debate (Lord and Oatley, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: GFRα1+ cells produce NGN3+/RARγ+ subset of undifferentiated spermatogonia.
source: The GFRα1+ cells produce NGN3+/RARγ+ subset of undifferentiated spermatogonia (composed of more Aaligned, and fewer Asingle and Apair) (Nakagawa et al., 2007) that differentiate into differentiating spermatogonia (Kit+) in response to retinoic acid.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: NGN3+/RARγ+ subset of undifferentiated spermatogonia differentiate into differentiating spermatogonia (Kit+) in response to retinoic acid.
source: The GFRα1+ cells produce NGN3+/RARγ+ subset of undifferentiated spermatogonia (composed of more Aaligned, and fewer Asingle and Apair) (Nakagawa et al., 2007) that differentiate into differentiating spermatogonia (Kit+) in response to retinoic acid.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Undifferentiated spermatogonia move within the basal compartment of the seminiferous tubules and regulate the balance between self-renewal and differentiation by competing for fibroblast growth factors (FGFs).
source: These undifferentiated spermatogonia move within the basal compartment of the seminiferous tubules and regulate the balance between self-renewal and differentiation by competing for fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) that are secreted from deferent niches (Kitadate et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Rac1-mediated cell migration is important for spermatogonial stem cell homing.
source: Although transplantation studies using in vitro cultured spermatogonial stem cells have reported that Rac1-mediated cell migration is important for spermatogonial stem cell homing (Takashima et al., 2011), the molecules that are involved in spermatogonia migration and their mechanisms have not been clarified (Kanamori et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: TEX14 is an important molecule for stability of ICBs.
source: TEX14 is an important molecule for stability of ICBs, which are essential for maintaining the structure of syncytia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: TEX14 localizes to germline ICBs and inhibits the final separation of the cytoplasm.
source: This protein localizes to germline ICBs and inhibits the final separation of the cytoplasm; in mice lacking this gene, the cytoplasm of male germ cells is completely separated causing spermatogenesis to be halted (Greenbaum et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: In mice lacking TEX14, the cytoplasm of male germ cells is completely separated causing spermatogenesis to be halted.
source: This protein localizes to germline ICBs and inhibits the final separation of the cytoplasm; in mice lacking this gene, the cytoplasm of male germ cells is completely separated causing spermatogenesis to be halted (Greenbaum et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The formation of syncytium is essential for spermatogenesis.
source: This result indicates that the formation of syncytium is essential for spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the TEX14 knockout phenotype.

claim: Seminolipids are important for the sustenance of ICB in spermatocytes.
source: Seminolipids, which are sulfated glycolipids, are important for the sustenance of ICB in spermatocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Mice lacking Ugt8a and Gal3st1 show an aggregation of spermatocytes.
source: This is evident in mice lacking the Ugt8a and Gal3st1, required for seminolipids synthesis, as they show an aggregation of spermatocytes (Fujimoto et al., 2000; Honke et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: A similar phenotype to Ugt8a and Gal3st1 knockout was observed in mice lacking the Stx2 gene.
source: Although the detailed molecular mechanism is unknown, a similar phenotype was observed in mice lacking the Stx2 gene (Fujiwara et al., 2013), which functions in the transport of seminolipids to the cell membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: STX2 functions in the transport of seminolipids to the cell membrane.
source: Although the detailed molecular mechanism is unknown, a similar phenotype was observed in mice lacking the Stx2 gene (Fujiwara et al., 2013), which functions in the transport of seminolipids to the cell membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: In humans, the loss of function of STX2 results in the failure of spermatogenesis with spermatocyte aggregation.
source: In humans, similar to that of mice, the loss of function of STX2 results in the failure of spermatogenesis with spermatocyte aggregation (Nakamura et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The exocyst complex is a heterodimeric protein complex composed of eight subunits (EXOC1–EXOC8).
source: In this study, we focus on the exocyst complex, a heterodimeric protein complex composed of eight subunits (EXOC1–EXOC8) that are widely conserved from yeast to humans (Koumandou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The exocyst complex is widely conserved from yeast to humans.
source: In this study, we focus on the exocyst complex, a heterodimeric protein complex composed of eight subunits (EXOC1–EXOC8) that are widely conserved from yeast to humans (Koumandou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Exocyst-mediated vesicle trafficking is crucial for cell division, morphogenesis, and cell migration.
source: Exocyst-mediated vesicle trafficking is crucial for various fundamental cellular phenomena such as cell division, morphogenesis, and cell migration.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In cytokinesis, the exocyst is localized to ICB.
source: In cytokinesis, the exocyst is localized to ICB (Neto et al., 2013) and is required for the transport of factors required for the final separation of the plasma membrane (Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The exocyst is required for the transport of factors required for the final separation of the plasma membrane.
source: In cytokinesis, the exocyst is localized to ICB (Neto et al., 2013) and is required for the transport of factors required for the final separation of the plasma membrane (Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The exocyst has been implicated in cell migration via the reconstitution of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: The exocyst has also been implicated in cell migration via the reconstitution of the actin cytoskeleton (Liu et al., 2012; Parrini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The exocyst is important for embryo development.
source: Although studies using gene-deficient mouse models have shown that the exocyst is important for embryo development (Mizuno et al., 2015; Friedrich et al., 1997; Fogelgren et al., 2015; Dickinson et al., 2016), its tissue-specific functions in adults are largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: In Drosophila models, the exocyst plays an important role in the formation of both female and male gametes.
source: In Drosophila models, the exocyst plays an important role in the formation of both female and male gametes (Giansanti et al., 2015; Wan et al., 2019; Murthy and Schwarz, 2004; Mao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: All exocyst subunits are expressed in male germ cells at each stage of differentiation in mice.
source: In mice, all exocyst subunits are expressed in male germ cells at each stage of differentiation (Green et al., 2018), and although it is predicted that these subunits may be involved in mammalian spermatogenesis, the function of these subunits is completely unknown.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to published data.

claim: PA-tagged EXOC1 protein was expressed in the adult testes of Exoc1+/PA-C and Exoc1+/PA-N mice.
source: We performed western blot analyses for the PA-tag in the testes of both Exoc1PA-C and Exoc1PA-N adult (10–20-week-old) mice and confirmed a band of the molecular size as expected (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No homozygous mutants were obtained in the Exoc1PA-C strain.
source: In the Exoc1PA-C strain, no homozygous mutants were obtained (0/20).
evidence: This is a direct observation from breeding experiments.

claim: Homozygous mutants were obtained in the Exoc1PA-N strain.
source: By contrast, in the Exoc1PA-N strain, homozygous mutants were obtained (9/27), and no abnormal phenotypes were found in them.
evidence: This is a direct observation from breeding experiments.

claim: Exoc1PA-N homozygous mutants showed no abnormal phenotypes.
source: By contrast, in the Exoc1PA-N strain, homozygous mutants were obtained (9/27), and no abnormal phenotypes were found in them.
evidence: This is a direct observation from phenotypic analysis.

claim: Progenies were obtained from crosses between Exoc1PA-N homozygous mutants.
source: Furthermore, progenies were obtained from crosses between Exoc1PA-N homozygous mutants.
evidence: This is a direct observation from breeding experiments.

claim: Exoc1 knock-out (KO) mice are early embryonic lethal.
source: As the Exoc1 knock-out (KO) mice are early embryonic lethal (Mizuno et al., 2015), this result suggests that the addition of the PA-tag connected to the N-terminus, linked by LG3, does not impair the function of EXOC1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The addition of the PA-tag connected to the N-terminus, linked by LG3, does not impair the function of EXOC1.
source: As the Exoc1 knock-out (KO) mice are early embryonic lethal (Mizuno et al., 2015), this result suggests that the addition of the PA-tag connected to the N-terminus, linked by LG3, does not impair the function of EXOC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the viability and fertility of Exoc1PA-N homozygous mutants.

claim: EXOC1-PA was detected in all male germ cells observed in the Exoc1+/PA-C adult mice.
source: In immunofluorescence, EXOC1-PA was also detected in all male germ cells observed in the Exoc1+/PA-C adult mice (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), while no signal could be detected in the Exoc1PA-N/PA-N mice using any method.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PA signals were detected in Sertoli cells in Exoc1+/PA-C adult mice.
source: In Exoc1+/PA-C adult mice, PA signals were also detected in Sertoli cells, which are located at the basal compartment of the seminiferous tubules and whose nucleus are euchromatic with a large nucleolus (França et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: EXOC1 protein is expressed in male mouse germ and Sertoli cells.
source: These data indicate that EXOC1 protein is expressed in male mouse germ and Sertoli cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the immunofluorescence and western blot data.

claim: No signal for PNA-lectin was detected in the Exoc1 cKO adult mice.
source: To investigate the spermatogenic potential of Exoc1 cKO mice, PNA-lectin staining to detect acrosome was performed; however, no signal was detected in the Exoc1 cKO adult mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by PNA-lectin staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Almost no spermatids and spermatozoa were observed in the testes of Exoc1 cKO mice.
source: When cell morphology was observed by H and E staining, although almost no spermatids and spermatozoa were observed in the testes of Exoc1 cKO mice, large multinucleated cells were observed in the lumen of seminiferous tubules (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Large multinucleated cells were observed in the lumen of seminiferous tubules in Exoc1 cKO mice.
source: When cell morphology was observed by H and E staining, although almost no spermatids and spermatozoa were observed in the testes of Exoc1 cKO mice, large multinucleated cells were observed in the lumen of seminiferous tubules (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Multinucleated cells in Exoc1 cKO mice lacked ICB structures.
source: Detailed observations by scanning electron microscopy revealed ICB in control mice, while multinucleated cells that lacked ICB structures were observed in Exoc1 cKO mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by scanning electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: More than 70% of the sections in Exoc1 cKO adult mice contained AGS.
source: More than 70% of the sections contained AGS, and approximately 20% contained neither AGS nor sperm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Less than 10% of the cross-sections in Exoc1 cKO adult mice contained sperms.
source: Although less than 10% of the cross-sections contained sperms, these sperms were considered to be derived from spermatogonia that did not undergo Cre-LoxP recombination.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data.

claim: No embryos with the cKO allele were found in the Exoc1 cKO group in in vitro fertilization experiments.
source: We confirmed the genotype of the generated blastocysts by in vitro fertilization of wild-type oocytes with sperms from the Exoc1 cKO or control (Exoc1flox/-) mice and found embryos with the cKO allele in the control group but not in the Exoc1 cKO group (0/16) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: γH2AX was observed in the nuclei of AGS in Exoc1 cKO mice.
source: γH2AX, a spermatocyte marker for the pachytene stage, was observed in the nuclei of AGS (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: No aggregation was observed in the differentiating spermatogonia, Kit+ syncytia in Exoc1 cKO mice.
source: In contrast, no aggregation was observed in the differentiating spermatogonia, Kit+ syncytia (0/214) (Figure 2F and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: All of the 336 AGS in Exoc1 cKO adult mice were observed within the luminal compartment.
source: In order to investigate the arrangement of AGS in the seminiferous tubules, H and E staining and immunofluorescence for CLDN11, a major component of SCTJ (Morita et al., 1999), were performed, and all of the 336 AGS in Exoc1 cKO adult mice were observed within the luminal compartment (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The AGS seen in Exoc1 cKO mice are spermatocytes.
source: These data suggest that the AGS seen in Exoc1 cKO mice are spermatocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the γH2AX staining and luminal compartment localization.

claim: Mouse EXOC1 binds to STX2.
source: The binding of the three proteins was confirmed in all in vitro experiments where each protein was immunoprecipitated (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mouse STX2 binds to SNAP23.
source: The binding of the three proteins was confirmed in all in vitro experiments where each protein was immunoprecipitated (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: EXOC1 binds to SNAP23 in vivo in adult mouse testis.
source: We then confirmed the binding of SNAP23 to EXOC1 in the adult Exoc1PA-N/PA-N testis with anti-Snap23 antibody available for immunoprecipitation. Consequently, it was confirmed that EXOC1 binds to SNAP23 in vivo (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sperms were found in frequent seminiferous tubules in adult Snap23 cKO mice.
source: H and E staining and immunofluorescence showed that AGS with γH2AX signals were observed in Snap23 cKO mice (Figure 3C–E). However, as many spermatocytes did not aggregate in Snap23 cKO mice, spermatozoa were also observed by H and E and PNA-lectin staining (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: AGS with γH2AX signals were observed in Snap23 cKO mice.
source: H and E staining and immunofluorescence showed that AGS with γH2AX signals were observed in Snap23 cKO mice (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Sperms were found in more than 70% of the seminiferous tubule sections in Snap23 cKO adult mice.
source: We evaluated the appearance of AGS in Snap23 cKO adult mice by the same method as in the Exoc1 cKO mice and found sperms in more than 70% of the seminiferous tubule sections (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: AGS were observed in about 10% of the sections in Snap23 cKO adult mice.
source: Although AGS were observed in about 10% of the sections, the number of AGS per area in those sections was approximately 10% of that in the Exoc1 cKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The number of AGS per area in Snap23 cKO sections was approximately 10% of that in the Exoc1 cKO mice.
source: Although AGS were observed in about 10% of the sections, the number of AGS per area in those sections was approximately 10% of that in the Exoc1 cKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Snap23 is partially responsible for the formation or maintenance of the spermatocyte syncytium.
source: In any case, Snap23 is partially responsible for the formation or maintenance of the spermatocyte syncytium.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial AGS phenotype in Snap23 cKO mice.

claim: EXOC1 regulates the formation of the correct syncytium structure in cooperation with STX2 and SNAP23.
source: These results suggest that EXOC1 regulates the formation of the correct syncytium structure in cooperation with STX2 and SNAP23.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding data and phenotypic similarities.

claim: The pseudopods of GFRα1+ spermatogonia in Exoc1 cKO adult mice were significantly shorter than that of control mice.
source: The pseudopods of GFRα1+ spermatogonia in Exoc1 cKO adult mice were significantly shorter than that of control mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GFRα1+ spermatogonia in Exoc1 cKO mice had significantly shorter pseudopods than those of wild-type and Stx2 KO.
source: Pseudopod length was quantitatively assessed by Sholl analysis: GFRα1+ spermatogonia in Exoc1 cKO mice had significantly shorter pseudopods than those of wild-type and Stx2 KO (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Stx2 KO pseudopods tended to be shorter than wild-type pseudopods (p=0.052).
source: The Stx2 KO pseudopods tended to be shorter than wild-type pseudopods (p=0.052) (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: EXOC1 functions in the pseudopod elongation of GFRα1+ spermatogonia partially dependently, but not completely dependently of STX2.
source: These results suggest that EXOC1 functions in the pseudopod elongation of GFRα1+ spermatogonia partially dependently, but not completely dependently of STX2.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of pseudopod lengths in Exoc1 cKO and Stx2 KO mice.

claim: Pseudopod elongation was inhibited in GFRα1+ Asingle spermatogonia of the Exoc1 cKO group compared to the control group.
source: In this experiment, pseudopod elongation was inhibited in GFRα1+ Asingle spermatogonia of the Exoc1 cKO group compared to the control group (Figure 4D and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The distance between the connected cells of Apair was significantly shorter in GFRα1+ Apair spermatogonia in the Exoc1 cKO group than in the control group.
source: The distance between the connected cells of Apair and Aaligned was significantly shorter in GFRα1+ Apair spermatogonia in the Exoc1 cKO group than in the control group (Figure 4E and F and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The distance between the connected cells of Aaligned was significantly shorter in GFRα1+ Aaligned spermatogonia in the Exoc1 cKO group than in the control group.
source: The distance between the connected cells of Apair and Aaligned was significantly shorter in GFRα1+ Apair spermatogonia in the Exoc1 cKO group than in the control group (Figure 4E and F and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of active-Rac1 tended to be stronger for the plasma membrane of GFRα1+ spermatogonia of Exoc1 cKO mice compared to control mice.
source: Therefore, immunofluorescence for active-Rac1 was performed to examine Rac1 activity in GFRα1+ spermatogonia of Exoc1 cKO adult mice, and as expected, the fluorescence intensity of active-Rac1 tended to be stronger for the plasma membrane of GFRα1+ spermatogonia of Exoc1 cKO mice compared to control mice (Figure 4G and H, and Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: EXOC1 may function in GFRα1+ spermatogonia pseudopod elongation by negatively regulating the activity of Rac1.
source: Therefore, EXOC1 may function in GFRα1+ spermatogonia pseudopod elongation by negatively regulating the activity of Rac1.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased active-Rac1 in Exoc1 cKO mice and known mechanisms from the literature.

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of GFRα1+ cells in Exoc1 cKO adult mice compared to the control mice.
source: Immunofluorescence with antibodies to GFRα1 and RARγ showed a significant increase in the number of GFRα1+ cells and a significant decrease in the number of RARγ+ cells in Exoc1 cKO adult mice compared to the control mice (Figure 5A and B and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the number of RARγ+ cells in Exoc1 cKO adult mice compared to the control mice.
source: Immunofluorescence with antibodies to GFRα1 and RARγ showed a significant increase in the number of GFRα1+ cells and a significant decrease in the number of RARγ+ cells in Exoc1 cKO adult mice compared to the control mice (Figure 5A and B and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: There was no noticeable difference in the total number of GFRα1+ and RARγ+ cells in Exoc1 cKO adult mice compared to the control mice.
source: In addition, no noticeable difference in the total number of both cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The number of Kit+ differentiating spermatogonia significantly decreased in the Exoc1 cKO group.
source: Additionally, the number of Kit+ differentiating spermatogonia significantly decreased in the Exoc1 cKO group (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exoc1 strongly regulates spermatogonial differentiation but not proliferation as much.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Exoc1 strongly regulates spermatogonial differentiation but not proliferation as much.
evidence: This is inferred from the changes in cell numbers and differentiation markers.

claim: Abnormalities in the spermatogonia are not a direct factor in the failure of spermatogenesis exhibited by the Exoc1 cKO mice.
source: However, the presence of the next stage of differentiation, spermatocytes, suggests that abnormalities in the spermatogonia are not a direct factor in the failure of spermatogenesis exhibited by the Exoc1 cKO mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that spermatocytes are present despite spermatogonial abnormalities.

claim: The most significant factor in spermatogenesis failure in Exoc1 cKO mice may be the aggregation of spermatocytes.
source: Since chromosome synapsis is suggested to be normal in meiosis, the most significant factor in spermatogenesis failure may be the aggregation of spermatocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal chromosome synapsis and the presence of AGS.

claim: Chromosome synapsis is normal in Exoc1 cKO spermatocytes.
source: SYCP1 and SYCP3 signals were co-localized in autosomal pairs of the spermatocytes from Exoc1 cKO mice. These results suggest that meiosis proceeds normally to synapsis in Exoc1-deficient spermatocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Impaired transport of sulfated glycolipids may cause spermatocyte aggregation in Exoc1 cKO mice.
source: As the localization of seminolipids to the plasma membrane is impaired in spermatocytes of Stx2repro34 mice (Fujiwara et al., 2013), similarly in Exoc1 cKO mice, impaired seminolipid transport may have caused for the aggregation of the spermatocytes.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known role of seminolipids and the phenotypic similarity to Stx2 mutants.

claim: Insufficient membrane addition may cause spermatocyte aggregation in Exoc1 cKO mice.
source: This suggests that spermatocyte aggregation in Exoc1 cKO mice is due to an impaired supply of cell membranes to facilitate cytokinesis.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known role of the exocyst in membrane addition during cytokinesis.

claim: Impaired transport of ESCRT proteins may cause spermatocyte aggregation in Exoc1 cKO mice.
source: This suggests that the exocyst complex is more important for recruitment of the ESCRT III complex to the ICB than for formation of ICB and that disruption of this recruitment in Exoc1 cKO spermatocytes may be responsible for the impaired secondary ingression event (Agromayor and Martin-Serrano, 2013) in cytokinesis.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known role of the exocyst in ESCRT transport in cultured cells.

claim: Spermatogonia in Exoc1 cKO mice are biased toward undifferentiated maintenance.
source: Analysis of the differentiation status of spermatogonia showed an increase in GFRα1+ spermatogonia and a decrease in RARγ+ spermatogonia in Exoc1 cKO mice, suggesting that spermatogonia are biased toward undifferentiated maintenance.
evidence: This is inferred from the changes in GFRα1+ and RARγ+ cell numbers.

claim: EXOC1 may regulate pseudopod elongation and migration in the undifferentiated spermatogonia by inactivating Rac1 via SH3BP1 transport.
source: Therefore, EXOC1 may regulate pseudopod elongation and migration in the undifferentiated spermatogonia by inactivating Rac1 via SH3BP1 transport; since there are no reports of Sh3bp1 KO mice, it will be necessary to investigate whether pseudopod elongation and migration are impaired when Sh3bp1 is deficient in undifferentiated spermatogonia.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known role of the exocyst in SH3BP1 transport in cultured cells and the observed Rac1 overactivation.

claim: Undifferentiated spermatogonia migration may be important for maintaining the balance between self-renewal and differentiation.
source: In addition, since undifferentiated spermatogonia move within the basal compartment of the seminiferous tubules and regulate the balance between self-renewal and differentiation by competing with each other for FGFs (Kitadate et al., 2019), undifferentiated spermatogonia migration may be important for maintaining the balance between self-renewal and differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from established knowledge about spermatogonial migration and FGF competition.

claim: The disruption of the balance between self-renewal and differentiation in Exoc1 cKO mice may have been caused secondary to impaired pseudopod elongation.
source: The disruption of this balance seen in Exoc1 cKO mice may have been caused secondary to impaired pseudopod elongation of the cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed pseudopod defects and differentiation imbalance.

claim: Exoc1 deficiency results in insufficient inactivation of Rac1 in undifferentiated spermatogonia and impaired pseudopod elongation.
source: In contrast, Exoc1 deficiency results in insufficient inactivation of Rac1 in undifferentiated spermatogonia and impaired its pseudopod elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed Rac1 overactivation and pseudopod defects.

claim: Undifferentiated spermatogonia that are restricted by migration may remain physically close to FGFs-producing cells and thus repeatedly self-renew, limiting their differentiation.
source: As a result, undifferentiated spermatogonia that are restricted by migration may remain physically close to FGFs-producing cells and thus repeatedly self-renew, limiting their differentiation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known role of FGFs in spermatogonial self-renewal and the observed migration defects.

claim: Spermatocytes of Stx2repro34 mice exhibit multinucleated AGS.
source: The spermatocytes of Stx2repro34 mice, a null mutant of the Stx2 gene encoding the SNARE protein, exhibit multinucleated AGS (Fujiwara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Both Stx2repro34 and Exoc1 cKO mice show similar phenotypes of multinucleated AGS and normal chromosome synapsis.
source: Both Stx2repro34 and Exoc1 cKO mice show similar phenotypes of multinucleated AGS and normal chromosome synapsis (Fujiwara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between the two mouse models.

claim: In yeast, Sec3 promotes membrane fusion between transport vesicles and the cell membrane by coordinating with Sso2 and Sec9.
source: In addition, in yeast, Sec3 (an ortholog of mouse Exoc1) promotes membrane fusion between transport vesicles and the cell membrane by coordinating with Sso2 (an ortholog of mouse Stx2) and another SNARE protein, Sec9 (an ortholog of mouse Snap23) (Yue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: In yeast, Sec3 directly interacts with Sso2 and promotes the Sso2–Sec9 binary complex formation.
source: In yeast, Sec3 directly interacts with Sso2 and promotes the Sso2–Sec9 binary complex formation (Yue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Snap23 KO mice are embryonically lethal.
source: As Snap23 KO mice have been reported to be embryonically lethal (Suh et al., 2011) and the effect of Snap23 depletion on adult male germ cells was unknown, we generated Snap23 cKO mice specifically for male germ cells under the control of Nanos3 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and tested for the appearance of spermatocyte AGS in the adult testes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The exocyst complex contributes to cell migration by promoting actin assembly.
source: In a study of cultured cells, the exocyst complex was noted to contribute to cell migration by promoting actin assembly (Liu et al., 2012) and GFRα1+ undifferentiated spermatogonia were observed to be moving within the basal compartment of the seminiferous tubules (Hara et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: GFRα1+ undifferentiated spermatogonia move within the basal compartment of the seminiferous tubules.
source: In a study of cultured cells, the exocyst complex was noted to contribute to cell migration by promoting actin assembly (Liu et al., 2012) and GFRα1+ undifferentiated spermatogonia were observed to be moving within the basal compartment of the seminiferous tubules (Hara et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Arp3 is not expressed in spermatogonia.
source: Although the exocyst contributes to pseudopod formation by promoting Arp2/3-mediated actin assembly (Liu et al., 2012), Arp3 is not expressed in spermatogonia (Lie et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Rac1 regulates pseudopod elongation and cell migration by regulating the reconstruction of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Thus, we focused on the Rho family GTPase Rac1, which regulates pseudopod elongation and cell migration by regulating the reconstruction of the actin cytoskeleton (Raftopoulou and Hall, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The exocyst is required for the transport of SH3BP1, which converts Rac1 from its active to inactive form.
source: The exocyst is required for the transport of SH3BP1, which converts Rac1 from its active to inactive form, and when the exocyst is impaired in cultured human cells, Rac1 is over-activated and pseudopod elongation and cell migration are inhibited (Parrini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: When the exocyst is impaired in cultured human cells, Rac1 is over-activated and pseudopod elongation and cell migration are inhibited.
source: The exocyst is required for the transport of SH3BP1, which converts Rac1 from its active to inactive form, and when the exocyst is impaired in cultured human cells, Rac1 is over-activated and pseudopod elongation and cell migration are inhibited (Parrini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: GFRα1+ cell migration dictates the state of spermatogonia differentiation.
source: GFRα1+ cell migration dictates the state of spermatogonia differentiation (Kitadate et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: RARγ+ cells are one differentiation step from GFRα1+ cells.
source: Therefore, we counted the numbers of GFRα1+ cells and RARγ+ cells, which are one differentiation step from GFRα1+ cells (Kitadate et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: In the pachytene stage, chromosome synapsis occurs and the synaptonemal complex is formed.
source: In the pachytene stage, chromosome synapsis occurs and the synaptonemal complex is formed (Heyting, 1996).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: SYCP1 and SYCP3 are components of the synaptonemal complex.
source: To confirm this synapsis, chromosomes of spermatocytes from Exoc1 adult cKO mice were spread and immunofluorescence was performed using antibodies against SYCP1 and SYCP3, which are components of the synaptonemal complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Meiosis proceeds normally to synapsis in Exoc1-deficient spermatocytes.
source: SYCP1 and SYCP3 signals were co-localized in autosomal pairs of the spermatocytes from Exoc1 cKO mice. These results suggest that meiosis proceeds normally to synapsis in Exoc1-deficient spermatocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of SYCP1 and SYCP3 signals.

claim: 90% of the glycolipids in the testes are seminolipids.
source: First, the impaired transport of sulfated glycolipids: 90% of the glycolipids in the testes are seminolipids (Ishizuka, 1997), and there are spermatocyte aggregates even in mice lacking the genes required for seminolipid biosynthesis (Ugt8a and Gal3st1) (Fujimoto et al., 2000; Honke et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The localization of seminolipids to the plasma membrane is impaired in spermatocytes of Stx2repro34 mice.
source: As the localization of seminolipids to the plasma membrane is impaired in spermatocytes of Stx2repro34 mice (Fujiwara et al., 2013), similarly in Exoc1 cKO mice, impaired seminolipid transport may have caused for the aggregation of the spermatocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Mutant Drosophila which lacks Exoc8 function shows little expansion of spermatocyte surface area causing the emergence of a defective cytokinetic ring in spermatocytes.
source: The exocyst localizes to ICB for local membrane addition (Neto et al., 2013), and mutant Drosophila, which lacks Exoc8 function, shows little expansion of spermatocyte surface area causing the emergence of a defective cytokinetic ring in spermatocytes (Giansanti et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: In cytokinesis, cells are separated by ESCRT proteins after the cleavage furrow is squeezed by a contractile ring.
source: Third, the impaired transport of endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT) proteins that functions in cell separation: in cytokinesis, cells are separated by ESCRT proteins after the cleavage furrow is squeezed by a contractile ring (Elia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: In cultured human cells, depletion of EXOC3 and EXOC4 impairs the transport of CHMP2B and CHMP4B to ICB and causes multinucleation.
source: In cultured human cells, depletion of EXOC3 and EXOC4 impairs the transport of CHMP2B and CHMP4B, subunits of the ESCRT III complex, to ICB and causes multinucleation (Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The exocyst complex is more important for recruitment of the ESCRT III complex to the ICB than for formation of ICB.
source: This suggests that the exocyst complex is more important for recruitment of the ESCRT III complex to the ICB than for formation of ICB and that disruption of this recruitment in Exoc1 cKO spermatocytes may be responsible for the impaired secondary ingression event (Agromayor and Martin-Serrano, 2013) in cytokinesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of the exocyst in ESCRT transport.

claim: Two genes encoding the ESCRT III complex subunit (Chmp2b and Chmp4c) KO mice are fertile.
source: On the Mouse Genome Informatics database (http://www.informatics.jax.org/), there are 10 genes encoding the ESCRT III complex subunit, and two of them (Chmp2b and Chmp4c) KO mice are fertile (Dickinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Nanos3-Cre mice express CRE from spermatogonia.
source: As Nanos3-Cre mice express CRE from spermatogonia (Suzuki et al., 2008), the Exoc1 cKO (Exoc1Flox/Flox:: Nanos3+/Cre) mice used in this study were models in which the Exoc1 gene was deficient from spermatogonia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Spermatocytes aggregated in Stx2 KO mice generated in this study.
source: In the Stx2 KO mice generated in this study, as in the Stx2repro34 mice (Fujiwara et al., 2013), spermatocytes were observed to aggregate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.
